domain_label: Plated-Jewelry Base-Metal Substrates — Mechanics, Skin-Safety, Tarnish & Quality-Cost Selection
purpose: A decision method for choosing the base-metal substrate under a plated fashion-jewelry piece (brass, sterling 925, stainless 316L, copper, zinc/pewter alloys) by grading each on mechanical/appearance properties, skin-safety and nickel release (EN1811 [FACT]), tarnish tendency and method-derived relative cost, so an agent can match a substrate to a price/quality target for 18-25 skin-contact wear without inventing prices, market shares or unverified hypoallergenic claims.
assumptions: the base metal is the load-bearing substrate UNDER a decorative plating (gold/vermeil/rhodium), so its cost, mechanics and skin-safety govern the piece even though the plating governs the visible surface; this KB owns the substrate, not the finish system (kb2) or the durability/value-engineering acceptance tests (kb3)

EN1811 (nickel-release reference test) and the EU REACH Annex XVII entry-27 migration limits (0.5 ug/cm2/week prolonged skin contact; 0.2 ug/cm2/week for post assemblies inserted into pierced ears) are cited public facts [FACT]; the US has no direct federal nickel-release limit, so nickel is a market/skin-safety fact here, not a US legal mandate

sterling silver = 92.5% Ag is the US FTC Jewelry Guides definition (16 CFR Part 23) [FACT]; rhodium is a hard, bright-white, tarnish-resistant platinum-group metal commonly plated over sterling silver and white gold [FACT], covered in depth in kb2

all relative-cost statements are ordinal (a ranking derived by [METHOD] from public commodity indices and silver spot) and never absolute per-piece prices; no market size, gold-plated-vs-solid share, demographic purchase rate or competitor price is asserted as measured
every claim is tagged [FACT] (with basis), [ESTIMATE] (with method + confidence), [METHOD] (a way to obtain the number) or [UNKNOWN]; the discipline mirrors the sweater_vertical landed-cost exemplar
exclusions: the finish systems themselves — gold plating / vermeil / gold-filled thresholds and rhodium-over-silver science (kb2_finishes_rhodium_gold owns those)

durability/adhesion/salt-spray/abrasion acceptance testing and the cost-vs-quality value-engineering curve (kb3_quality_cost_value_engineering owns those; this KB only names which tests gate a substrate claim)
deposition physics, bath chemistry and plating-line engineering (the supply-side electro-plating / pvd-sputtering taxonomy owns those)

actual US market numbers — how many buy, what percent is gold-plated, which ethnicity or which brands — which are produced later by the market specialist's polls and public-data pulls, never guessed here
pricing, margin and COGS build-up for a finished piece (the economics specialist owns those; this KB stops at ordinal substrate cost rank)

competency_questions.question: What role does the base-metal substrate play in a plated piece, and which axes must every candidate metal be graded on?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBSTRATE_ROLE_FRAME states the substrate carries cost, mechanics, tarnish and skin-safety while the plating carries appearance, and PROPERTY_AXES_FRAMEWORK names the grading axes (formability/hardness, heft/appearance, tarnish tendency, nickel-release risk, plateability, method-derived relative cost)

competency_questions.question: What is the EN1811 nickel-release fact and its migration limits, and how is nickel release measured?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NICKEL_RELEASE_EN1811 states EN1811 as the reference test, the REACH entry-27 limits (0.5 ug/cm2/week prolonged contact, 0.2 for pierced-ear posts) [FACT], the DMG spot test as the field screen, and that nickel is the most common contact allergen

competency_questions.question: Why do nickel and 'hypoallergenic' matter specifically for 18-25 skin-contact wear, and what is the nickel-free vs nickel-safe distinction?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SKIN_CONTACT_1825_RATIONALE states that earrings/piercings are prolonged and broken-skin contact, that nickel sensitization is prevalent and lifelong, that 'hypoallergenic' is an unregulated marketing term, and separates nickel-free (no nickel present) from nickel-safe (release below the EN1811 limit) [FACT]

competency_questions.question: By what mechanisms does each base metal tarnish or corrode, and why does that matter under a thin plating?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TARNISH_CORROSION_MECHANISMS states silver-sulfide tarnish on sterling, copper oxide/carbonate (green) on copper/brass, dezincification and season cracking of brass, and the galvanic couple at plating pores/cracks (small base-metal anode, large noble-gold cathode) driving accelerated attack and skin discoloration [FACT]

competency_questions.question: What are brass's properties, tradeoffs and skin/plating implications as a substrate?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BRASS_SUBSTRATE states cartridge brass (Cu-Zn, e.g. CDA 260) / jeweler's bronze as cheap, castable and formable, tarnish-prone (dezincification, season cracking), usually low-nickel but copper-interdiffusing so needing a nickel/palladium barrier under gold [FACT/ESTIMATE]

competency_questions.question: What are sterling 925's properties and why is it the premium substrate for rhodium/vermeil finishes?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: STERLING_925_SUBSTRATE states 92.5% Ag [FACT-FTC], nickel-free, tarnish-prone via silver sulfide (motivating rhodium), the dearest common substrate, and the required base for a legitimate vermeil (>=10k gold, >=2.5um over sterling) claim

competency_questions.question: Why is stainless 316L 'surgical steel' nickel-safe but not nickel-free, and what does that mean for a hypoallergenic claim?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: STAINLESS_316L_SUBSTRATE states 316L contains ~10-14% nickel yet its passive chromium-oxide film keeps nickel release low (nickel-safe, not nickel-free), that 'surgical steel' is marketing, and that a hypoallergenic claim still needs EN1811 evidence not the label [FACT]

competency_questions.question: What are the properties and risks of copper and of zinc/pewter alloy substrates, and where do they belong?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COPPER_SUBSTRATE states soft, cheap, easily formed, high-tarnish, gold-interdiffusing (needs nickel barrier); ZINC_PEWTER_ALLOY_SUBSTRATE states low-melt castable zamak/pewter for cheap costume casting, soft and dense (heft), with lead/cadmium regulatory exposure and plating-adhesion needs [FACT/ESTIMATE]

competency_questions.question: Which substrates need a barrier underplate before gold, how plateable is each, and how do you keep the barrier hypoallergenic?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BARRIER_UNDERPLATE_NEED states copper/brass interdiffusion requires a nickel (or nickel-free palladium / white-bronze) barrier, and PLATEABILITY_ADHESION states stainless needs a Wood's nickel strike, zinc/pewter a cyanide/alkaline copper strike, and brass/copper plate readily [FACT]

competency_questions.question: How is the relative cost of the base metals obtained honestly, without inventing a price?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RELATIVE_COST_METHOD gives an ordinal ranking (zinc/brass cheapest, copper low, stainless cheap-raw-but-costly-to-process, sterling dearest tracking silver spot) derived by [METHOD] from public commodity indices (LME copper/zinc/nickel, silver spot) plus a formability/labor adjustment, and states no absolute per-piece price is asserted

competency_questions.question: Why does substrate skin-safety still matter under a plating, and how is it verified after wear-through?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WEAR_THROUGH_SKIN_SAFETY states that plating pores/scratches/wear expose the base metal to skin, that a nickel interlayer or nickel-bearing substrate can then exceed the EN1811 limit, and that an EN1811 retest after wear/abrasion (not the as-made surface) is the honest gate for a skin-safety claim [FACT]

competency_questions.question: Which base metal fits which price/quality target, and why is there no single 'best' base metal?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRICE_QUALITY_TARGET_MATRIX maps targets (low-cost costume, mid fashion, hypoallergenic-forward, rhodium/vermeil premium) to substrates using cost, skin-safety, appearance/heft and formability, and APPEARANCE_HEFT_PERCEPTION and FORMABILITY_MECHANICAL supply the perception and mechanical inputs, with the choice stated as target-dependent

competency_questions.question: What US lead/cadmium regulatory limits bear on cheap zinc/pewter substrates and skin-contact jewelry?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REGULATORY_LEAD_CADMIUM states the CPSC total-lead limit for children's products (100 ppm) and state metal-jewelry lead/cadmium limits (e.g. California AB 1681 / Prop 65) as facts that constrain zinc/pewter/pot-metal and disqualify legacy leaded pewter for body-contact pieces [FACT]

competency_questions.question: How is the FACT/ESTIMATE/UNKNOWN discipline enforced, and what does this KB hand to the finishes and quality-cost KBs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HONESTY_LEDGER separates the [FACT] anchors (EN1811, sterling 92.5%, 316L nickel content, lead limits) from the [ESTIMATE] cost ranks and [UNKNOWN] live prices, and SUBSTRATE_HANDOFF delivers a per-target substrate shortlist with its skin-safety and barrier conditions to kb2/kb3

glossary.definition: The structural metal that forms the body of a plated jewelry piece and is covered by a thin decorative finish; here brass, sterling silver 925, stainless 316L, copper, or a zinc/pewter casting alloy. It governs cost, weight/heft, formability, tarnish and — at any plating pore, scratch or wear-through — the metal that actually contacts skin.

EN1811 is the European reference test that measures how much nickel migrates from an item per unit area per week; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 27 caps release at 0.5 ug/cm2/week for prolonged skin contact and 0.2 ug/cm2/week for post assemblies inserted into pierced ears [FACT]. The dimethylglyoxime (DMG) spot test is the quick qualitative field screen. The US has no equivalent federal release limit, so nickel is a skin-safety and market fact here, not a US legal mandate.

Nickel-free means no nickel is present in the alloy or stack; nickel-safe (or release-compliant) means nickel may be present but its measured release is below the EN1811 limit. 316L stainless is nickel-safe (passive-film-protected) but NOT nickel-free (~10-14% Ni). Conflating the two is a common and consequential error for a sensitized wearer.

A marketing term with no binding legal definition in the US; it does not guarantee nickel-free or nickel-safe status. A defensible hypoallergenic claim for a skin-contact piece rests on an EN1811 nickel-release result (ideally after simulated wear), not on the word itself.

An alloy of 92.5% silver with ~7.5% other metal (usually copper), the US FTC Jewelry Guides (16 CFR Part 23) threshold for calling a piece 'sterling' [FACT]. Nickel-free but tarnish-prone (silver sulfide); the standard premium substrate under rhodium (to stay bright white) and the required base for a legitimate vermeil claim.

A low-carbon austenitic Cr-Ni-Mo stainless (~16-18% Cr, ~10-14% Ni, ~2-3% Mo) whose self-healing chromium-oxide passive film gives it low nickel release and good corrosion resistance. 'Surgical steel' is a marketing phrase, not a purity guarantee; it is nickel-safe, not nickel-free, and hard to form and to plate (needs an activation strike).

Copper-zinc alloys (cartridge brass CDA 260 ~70Cu/30Zn; jeweler's bronze/gilding metal is a high-copper brass). Cheap, castable and formable, usually low-nickel, but tarnish-prone (dezincification, stress-corrosion 'season cracking') and copper-interdiffusing, so it needs a nickel or nickel-free barrier under gold.

Low-melting cast alloys for cheap costume jewelry: zinc die-cast ('zamak', 'pot metal') and tin-based pewter (historically leaded). Easy and cheap to cast into detailed shapes, soft and dense (reads as heft), but with lead/cadmium regulatory exposure and plating-adhesion challenges requiring a copper strike.

A metal layer (classically bright/sulfamate nickel, or nickel-free palladium / white bronze Cu-Sn-Zn) deposited between a copper-bearing substrate and the gold finish to stop copper interdiffusion (which stains and dulls thin gold) and to level the surface. Nickel is the best barrier but reintroduces a nickel-release risk if it becomes skin-exposed at an edge or wear point.

Where a plating has pores, cracks or wear-through, the small exposed base-metal area (anode) is coupled to the large noble gold surface (cathode), accelerating localized corrosion of the base metal and producing green/black skin marks and, if a nickel layer is exposed, elevated nickel release [FACT].

An ordinal ranking of substrate material cost obtained by pulling public commodity references (LME copper/zinc/nickel, silver spot) and adjusting for formability/processing labor, expressed as a rank (zinc/brass cheapest -> copper -> stainless raw-cheap-but-process-costly -> sterling dearest), never as an invented absolute per-piece price.

nodes.definition: Frame what the base-metal substrate is and why it, not the visible plating, decides most of a piece's economics and safety. In a plated fashion piece the thin gold/rhodium finish owns appearance while the base metal owns cost, weight/heft, formability, tarnish behavior and — critically — the metal that touches skin at any plating pore, scratch or wear-through. The five substrates this KB grades are brass (Cu-Zn), sterling 925 (92.5% Ag [FACT-FTC]), stainless 316L, copper, and zinc/pewter casting alloys. This node fixes the scope boundary: this KB owns substrate selection; kb2 owns the finish systems (gold/vermeil/rhodium) and kb3 owns durability testing and the cost-vs-quality curve. Getting the substrate wrong cannot be fixed by the finish, because the finish is microns thin and the base metal outlives it in wear.

included: the substrate-vs-finish division of responsibility
the five candidate base metals as the graded set
the KB scope boundary against kb2 (finishes) and kb3 (durability/value)
excluded: durability acceptance testing and the cost-quality curve (kb3)

pros.claim: Framing the substrate as the load-bearing, skin-contacting layer stops the plating from being credited with properties (cost, safety, wear) it cannot deliver on a microns-thin film
pros.example: a $1 zinc casting under 0.5um of gold is still a $1 zinc piece the moment the plating wears at a contact point

cons.claim: Separating substrate from finish is an abstraction; real durability and skin-safety are a stack property that only kb2/kb3 fully close
cons.example: whether a brass ring is skin-safe depends jointly on the barrier and topcoat that kb2 specifies

letting substrate choice drift into finish or durability scope this node explicitly hands to kb2/kb3

nodes.definition: State the anchoring skin-safety fact. EN1811 is the European reference test measuring nickel migration per unit area per week; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 27 caps release at 0.5 ug/cm2/week for items in prolonged skin contact and 0.2 ug/cm2/week for post assemblies inserted into pierced ears [FACT]. Nickel is the single most common contact allergen; sensitization is prevalent (higher in women) and, once acquired, lifelong. The dimethylglyoxime (DMG) spot test is the fast qualitative field screen for nickel release (pink = fail), while EN1811 is the quantitative lab method. Note the jurisdiction fact: the US has NO equivalent federal nickel-release limit, so for a US venture nickel control is a skin-safety and market-differentiator fact, not a legal mandate — which is exactly why an honest [FACT] basis matters instead of a borrowed legal claim.

included: EN1811 as the reference test and the REACH 0.5 / 0.2 ug/cm2/week limits
the DMG spot test as the field screen
nickel as the most common contact allergen and the no-US-federal-limit jurisdiction fact

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a nickel-release limit or reference test changes

pros.claim: Anchoring on the actual EN1811 numbers and their jurisdiction lets every downstream skin-safety claim cite a real standard instead of a vague 'hypoallergenic' promise
pros.example: a DMG-screened, EN1811-passing post can be described precisely as nickel-safe under 0.2 ug/cm2/week rather than just 'hypoallergenic'

cons.claim: EN1811 is a European standard with no US legal force, so it disciplines a claim but does not by itself compel compliance in the US market
cons.example: a US seller can legally ship high-nickel-release pieces, so nickel control is a chosen quality bar, not a mandate

failure_modes: citing EN1811/REACH as if it were binding US law
confusing the 0.5 prolonged-contact limit with the stricter 0.2 pierced-post limit
acceptance_tests: EN1811, the 0.5 and 0.2 ug/cm2/week REACH limits, the DMG spot test and the no-US-federal-limit fact are all stated with correct basis
revisit_triggers: REACH nickel limits are revised or a US federal nickel-release rule is introduced
a state adopts a nickel-in-jewelry limit

nodes.definition: Explain why nickel and 'hypoallergenic' matter acutely for the owner's 18-25 skin-contact audience. Earrings and body jewelry involve prolonged and often broken-skin contact (a fresh or healing piercing is an open wound), the exact conditions the stricter EN1811 pierced-post limit (0.2 ug/cm2/week) targets. Nickel allergic contact dermatitis presents as itching, redness and eczema at the contact site; sensitization is prevalent and lifelong, so a bad first experience durably removes a young buyer. 'Hypoallergenic' is an unregulated marketing term [FACT] that promises nothing measurable. The load-bearing distinction: nickel-free (no nickel present) vs nickel-safe (nickel present but release below the EN1811 limit) [FACT]. For a skin-contact SKU aimed at this cohort, the substrate/stack should be demonstrably one of the two, evidenced by test — not merely labelled hypoallergenic. How many of the cohort are nickel-sensitized is a real prevalence number to pull from dermatology literature [METHOD], not to guess.

included: prolonged/broken-skin contact of earrings and piercings
nickel dermatitis and lifelong sensitization as a durable churn risk
the nickel-free vs nickel-safe distinction and 'hypoallergenic' as unregulated

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: cohort sensitization data, product mix, or a hypoallergenic definition changes

pros.claim: Tying the cohort's wear mode to the stricter pierced-post limit makes skin-safety a concrete design requirement rather than a slogan
pros.example: specifying a nickel-safe post evidenced at <0.2 ug/cm2/week directly serves an 18-25 earring buyer with pierced ears

cons.claim: Sensitization prevalence in the exact cohort is a literature number, not a fact this KB owns, so the size of the risk is [METHOD]-to-pull not asserted
cons.example: the share of 18-25 US women who are nickel-sensitized must be cited from dermatology studies, not estimated here

failure_modes: treating 'hypoallergenic' as a guarantee of skin-safety
applying the 0.5 prolonged-contact limit to pierced-ear posts that need the 0.2 limit
guessing a cohort sensitization rate instead of pulling it [METHOD]
acceptance_tests: the prolonged/broken-skin wear mode, the lifelong-sensitization churn risk, 'hypoallergenic' as unregulated, and the nickel-free vs nickel-safe distinction are all stated, with cohort prevalence flagged [METHOD]
revisit_triggers: new dermatology prevalence data for the cohort is pulled
the product mix shifts toward or away from pierced-ear posts
a regulator defines 'hypoallergenic'

nodes.definition: Establish the corrosion/tarnish mechanisms that differentiate the substrates and that a thin plating only postpones. Sterling silver tarnishes by forming silver sulfide (Ag2S, black/yellow) when it reacts with atmospheric and skin sulfur compounds — the exact reason rhodium plating (kb2) is used to keep silver bright. Copper and high-copper brass form copper oxides/carbonates (dulling, then green/verdigris) and can leave green skin marks. Brass additionally suffers dezincification (selective zinc loss weakening the alloy) and stress-corrosion 'season cracking' in ammonia/humid environments. Zinc/pewter alloys corrode and can bloom white. The stack-level mechanism that ties these to plated jewelry is the galvanic couple at plating pores/cracks: a small exposed base-metal anode coupled to the large noble-gold cathode accelerates localized attack and, where a nickel layer is exposed, raises nickel release [FACT]. Tarnish tendency is therefore both an appearance axis and a skin-safety axis.

included: silver-sulfide tarnish, copper oxide/green, brass dezincification/season cracking, zinc bloom
the galvanic couple at plating pores/cracks
tarnish as both an appearance and skin-safety axis

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a finish/topcoat change or a new corrosion mode alters tarnish behavior

pros.claim: Naming the specific corrosion chemistry per metal makes tarnish a predictable design axis instead of a vague 'it goes dull' worry
pros.example: knowing sterling tarnishes via Ag2S explains precisely why rhodium (kb2) is the fix, not a heavier gold layer

cons.claim: Real tarnish rate depends on the finish, topcoat and the wearer's chemistry, which this substrate node does not fully model
cons.example: the same brass tarnishes far slower under an e-coat topcoat that kb2 owns

failure_modes: treating tarnish as purely cosmetic and missing the galvanic/skin-marking consequence at pores
attributing brass failure to plain oxidation when dezincification or season cracking is the mechanism
acceptance_tests: the per-metal tarnish mechanisms (Ag2S, copper green, dezincification/season cracking, zinc bloom) and the galvanic-couple-at-pores mechanism are stated
revisit_triggers: a topcoat/finish change (kb2) materially alters realized tarnish
a new substrate with different corrosion chemistry is added
field returns show a tarnish mode not modelled here

nodes.definition: Define the grading framework every candidate substrate is scored on, so selection is a comparable multi-axis judgment rather than a single-attribute preference. The axes: (1) formability/hardness (can it be cast, drawn, bent, and take posts?); (2) heft/appearance (density signals perceived quality; base color shows through thin plating); (3) tarnish/corrosion tendency (from TARNISH_CORROSION_MECHANISMS); (4) nickel-release / skin-safety risk (from NICKEL_RELEASE_EN1811); (5) plateability and barrier need; (6) method-derived relative cost. Each metal is strong on some axes and weak on others — there is no universal winner — which is why the output is a target-dependent matrix, not a ranking. This node is the schema the per-metal nodes populate and the target matrix later reads.

nodes.definition: Profile brass as the workhorse fashion-jewelry substrate. Cartridge brass (Cu-Zn, e.g. CDA 260 ~70/30) and high-copper 'jeweler's bronze'/gilding metal are inexpensive, readily cast, stamped and drawn, and take plating well — the default for mid-market plated pieces. Weaknesses: it tarnishes (copper oxidation to green, plus dezincification and stress-corrosion 'season cracking' from TARNISH_CORROSION_MECHANISMS), and because copper interdiffuses into gold and stains it, brass needs a barrier underplate (nickel, or nickel-free palladium/white bronze) before the gold finish. Nickel content of plain brass is typically low, so the nickel-release risk of a brass piece usually comes from a nickel barrier layer, not the brass itself — which makes the barrier choice (BARRIER_UNDERPLATE_NEED) the real skin-safety lever. Cost rank: among the cheapest [ESTIMATE-ordinal, from RELATIVE_COST_METHOD].

the copper-interdiffusion barrier need and low intrinsic nickel

nodes.definition: Profile sterling silver 925 as the premium substrate. Sterling is 92.5% silver with ~7.5% (usually copper), the US FTC Jewelry Guides threshold for the word 'sterling' (16 CFR Part 23) [FACT]. It is nickel-free (a genuine skin-safety advantage) and has a bright white base color, but it tarnishes readily via silver sulfide — which is precisely why rhodium plating (a hard, bright, tarnish-resistant platinum-group metal) is applied over sterling to keep it white and bright (kb2). It is by a wide margin the dearest of the five substrates and its cost tracks the volatile silver spot price [METHOD-pull spot, do not fabricate]. Its defining role here: sterling is the required base for a legitimate 'vermeil' claim (FTC: >=10k gold, >=2.5um thick, over sterling) and the standard base under rhodium — so choosing sterling is usually a finish-driven, premium-tier decision, not a cost-driven one.

nodes.definition: Profile stainless 316L and correct the 'surgical steel' myth. 316L is a low-carbon austenitic Cr-Ni-Mo stainless (~16-18% Cr, ~10-14% Ni, ~2-3% Mo). Its self-healing chromium-oxide passive film gives excellent corrosion/tarnish resistance and LOW nickel release — so it is typically nickel-SAFE (release below EN1811) but NOT nickel-FREE (it contains substantial nickel). 'Surgical steel' is a marketing phrase, not a purity or release guarantee [FACT]. Strengths: hard, corrosion- and tarnish-resistant, cheap as raw material, and often worn bare (no plating needed) which sidesteps wear-through entirely. Weaknesses: it is hard to cold-form and to plate — plating needs an activation strike (Wood's nickel) because the passive film otherwise causes adhesion failure. The honest rule: a 316L hypoallergenic claim rests on an EN1811 result, especially if the passive film is compromised by scratching or wear, not on the 'surgical' label.

included: 316L composition with ~10-14% nickel and the passive film giving low release

nodes.definition: Profile copper. Pure copper is soft, highly formable, cheap and a good electrical/plating substrate, but it is the most tarnish-prone of the practical bases (oxide dulling, then green carbonate) and the classic green-skin culprit. Because copper interdiffuses rapidly into gold and stains it, copper (like brass) mandates a barrier underplate (nickel or nickel-free palladium/white bronze) before any gold. In plated jewelry copper appears in two roles: occasionally as the visible substrate for copper-toned or antiqued pieces, and very commonly as an underplate/leveling layer beneath the barrier on other substrates. Its softness is a double-edged property: excellent for intricate forming, poor for anything needing spring or wear resistance (a plain copper post bends and tarnishes). nodes.definition: Profile the cast pot-metals: zinc die-cast ('zamak') and tin-based pewter. These low-melting alloys are the cheapest route to detailed cast shapes at volume — the backbone of low-tier costume jewelry — and their density gives pieces a satisfying heft that is easily mistaken for quality (APPEARANCE_HEFT_PERCEPTION). Weaknesses are serious: they are soft and low-strength (bends, dents), corrode/bloom, and carry a real regulatory exposure because historically pewter was leaded and pot-metal can contain lead and cadmium — squarely in scope of US lead/cadmium jewelry limits (REGULATORY_LEAD_CADMIUM). Plating adhesion is harder than on brass and needs an alkaline/cyanide copper strike and careful surface prep. nodes.definition: Determine which substrates need a barrier underplate before gold and how to keep that barrier hypoallergenic. Copper and high-copper brass interdiffuse into thin gold, staining and dulling it, so they require a barrier layer between substrate and gold; sterling and 316L are less demanding but often still get an intermediate layer for adhesion/leveling. The classic barrier is bright or sulfamate nickel — cheap, an excellent diffusion barrier and leveller — but nickel under a thin/pored/worn gold layer is a latent skin-safety liability the moment it becomes skin-exposed (WEAR_THROUGH_SKIN_SAFETY). The nickel-free alternatives, which preserve a hypoallergenic stack, are palladium or palladium-nickel(low-Ni) and white bronze (Cu-Sn-Zn) [FACT]. The decision rule: copper/brass MUST have a barrier; whether that barrier is nickel or nickel-free is the pivotal skin-safety choice for a skin-contact SKU, trading cost (nickel cheap, palladium dear) against nickel-release risk.

nodes.definition: Grade how readily each substrate accepts and holds plating, because poor adhesion is a hidden cost and a durability/skin-safety failure. Brass and copper plate readily with standard cleaning and a strike. Zinc die-cast and pewter need careful prep and an alkaline/cyanide copper strike to build an adherent base before nickel/gold, and are unforgiving of surface contamination. Stainless 316L is the hardest: its chromium-oxide passive film must be activated (classically a Wood's nickel strike, or a sulfamate-nickel alternative) or the plating simply fails adhesion. Sterling plates well and is the standard rhodium base. The consequence for this KB: plateability is a real selection axis — a substrate that is cheap in raw form (316L, zinc) can be more expensive and defect-prone to plate, and adhesion failures later expose the base metal to skin (feeding WEAR_THROUGH_SKIN_SAFETY). nodes.definition: Close the loop between substrate and skin: a plating is microns thin and develops pores, scratches and wear points, at which the base metal (or the barrier layer) contacts skin — so substrate skin-safety is not made irrelevant by plating, only postponed. nodes.definition: Model the appearance and heft axis, where perception diverges from real quality. nodes.definition: Match substrate mechanics to what each jewelry category demands, because a metal ideal for casting can be wrong for a spring post. nodes.definition: State the US lead/cadmium regulatory facts that constrain cheap cast substrates and skin-contact jewelry. conflict_axes.name: cheapest_metal_vs_skin_safety
conflict_axes.description: The cheapest substrates and barriers (zinc/pewter, brass, nickel barrier) pull against the skin-safety gate for pieces in prolonged skin contact.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: for skin-contact SKUs the worn EN1811 gate wins; spend on a nickel-free barrier or nickel-safe substrate rather than ship a cheaper piece that fails worn

conflict_axes.name: nickel_content_vs_nickel_release
conflict_axes.description: 316L contains substantial nickel yet is nickel-safe by release; content-based and release-based judgments give opposite verdicts.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use measured release, not content, as the criterion; call 316L nickel-safe (never nickel-free) and re-verify after wear for highly sensitized wearers

conflict_axes.name: tarnish_prone_premium_vs_stable_cheap
conflict_axes.description: Sterling is premium and nickel-free but tarnishes; brass/316L are cheaper or stabler but not the same premium base.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: choose sterling only when the finish claim (vermeil/rhodium-over-silver/nickel-free premium) requires it; otherwise a barriered brass or a stable 316L serves better per cost

conflict_axes.name: heft_perception_vs_true_quality
conflict_axes.description: Consumers read weight as quality, but dense pot-metal is soft and low-durability while a light brass/316L piece can outlast it.
poles: choose dense substrate for perceived quality
choose durable substrate for real quality
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use heft as an honest marketing lever only after skin-safety, mechanical and lead/cadmium vetoes pass; never equate heft with durability

conflict_axes.name: nickel_free_vs_nickel_safe_route
conflict_axes.description: A hypoallergenic promise can be met by a nickel-free stack (dearer palladium/white-bronze barrier or sterling) or a nickel-safe one (316L, nickel barrier passing EN1811).
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: pick by claim and cost: nickel-free is the safest marketing position but costs more; nickel-safe is acceptable if EN1811-after-wear is evidenced and disclosed honestly

conflict_axes.name: formability_vs_durability
conflict_axes.description: Soft, easily-formed metals (copper, annealed brass, zinc) fight hard, springy, durable ones (316L, hardened brass) across categories.
poles: hard/springy for posts and durable rings
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: let the category's mechanical demand veto: castings/wire-work favor soft metals, posts/everyday rings favor hard/springy ones, independent of cost

conflict_axes.name: raw_cheap_vs_finished_cost
conflict_axes.description: A raw-cheap substrate (316L, zinc) can be plating-expensive and defect-prone, inverting a naive raw-material cost ranking.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: rank on finished cost by adding the activation-strike/copper-strike and yield penalty to the raw price before comparing tiers

conflict_axes.name: single_best_metal_vs_target_dependent
conflict_axes.description: Stakeholders want one 'best base metal' answer, but the axes make the best choice depend on the price/quality/skin-safety target.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: deliver the target-indexed matrix, not a single verdict; each target cell is justified on the six axes with lead/cadmium and mechanical vetoes

conflict_axes.name: nickel_barrier_performance_vs_hypoallergenic
conflict_axes.description: Nickel is the best, cheapest diffusion barrier under gold but reintroduces a nickel-release liability if it becomes skin-exposed at an edge or wear point.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: on skin-contact SKUs promising hypoallergenic, use a nickel-free barrier (palladium/white bronze); reserve the nickel barrier for non-skin-critical or robustly-covered geometry

edge_cases.description: 316L 'surgical steel' is sold as hypoallergenic to a nickel-sensitized buyer, but a scratched/worn passive film or exposed base locally exceeds the release limit
edge_cases.trigger: a hypoallergenic claim rests on the 'surgical steel' label with no EN1811-after-wear evidence
edge_cases.mitigation: back the claim with an EN1811 result after simulated wear and call it nickel-safe, not nickel-free

edge_cases.description: A zinc die-cast or pewter piece contains lead/cadmium above the CPSC/state limit for a body-contact or children's item
edge_cases.trigger: leaded pot-metal or legacy pewter is used without a composition test
edge_cases.mitigation: specify low-lead/low-cadmium alloy and composition-test each lot against CPSC 100 ppm / state limits before use

edge_cases.description: A bare brass or copper earring post contacts skin and releases copper (green marking) or, via a nickel barrier, nickel causing dermatitis
edge_cases.trigger: a skin-contact post is left unplated or under-barriered
edge_cases.mitigation: use a nickel-safe/nickel-free skin-contact surface and verify the worst-case exposed layer by EN1811

edge_cases.description: Gold is plated directly on copper or brass with no barrier, so copper interdiffuses and stains/dulls the gold
edge_cases.trigger: the barrier underplate is omitted on a copper-bearing substrate
edge_cases.mitigation: always deposit a nickel or nickel-free barrier between a copper-bearing substrate and the gold

edge_cases.description: 'Hypoallergenic' is claimed on a piece with no nickel-release test, treating the unregulated term as a guarantee
edge_cases.trigger: a marketing claim substitutes the word for an EN1811/DMG result
edge_cases.mitigation: require an EN1811 (or DMG screen) result before any hypoallergenic claim; disclose nickel-safe vs nickel-free honestly

edge_cases.description: A sterling substrate under thin gold tarnishes (silver sulfide) because no rhodium/barrier protects it
edge_cases.trigger: sterling is plated with gold only, with no rhodium or barrier against sulfur
edge_cases.mitigation: protect sterling with rhodium or a barrier/topcoat (kb2) where tarnish is a concern

edge_cases.description: A per-piece substrate price is quoted as measured, or a market/plated-vs-solid share is stated as fact
edge_cases.trigger: an absolute cost or market number is asserted instead of tagged [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD]/[UNKNOWN]
edge_cases.mitigation: keep cost ordinal, pull live spot by [METHOD], and route market/share numbers to the market specialist as [METHOD]/[UNKNOWN]

edge_cases.description: Brass in a humid/sweat or ammonia environment dezincifies or season-cracks, cracking the plating over it
edge_cases.trigger: brass is used in a high-humidity or cleaner-exposed application without accounting for stress-corrosion
edge_cases.mitigation: control residual stress and use a suitable brass grade/finish; flag season-cracking risk in the substrate spec

edge_cases.description: A heavy zinc/pewter piece is marketed as 'solid'/high-quality on heft while being soft, low-durability pot-metal
edge_cases.trigger: heft is presented as proof of quality
edge_cases.mitigation: use heft only as an honest feel descriptor after durability and skin-safety pass; do not equate it with quality

edge_cases.description: A nickel barrier chosen for performance sits on a high-wear edge where the gold wears through and exposes the nickel to skin
edge_cases.trigger: a nickel barrier is used on a skin-contact, high-wear geometry with a thin gold cover
edge_cases.mitigation: switch to a nickel-free barrier on skin-contact high-wear geometry, or increase cover and verify by worn EN1811

edge_cases.description: 316L is chosen for hypoallergenic reasons but the part needs forming/plating the hard, passive-filmed steel resists, causing adhesion or forming failure
edge_cases.trigger: 316L is selected on skin-safety alone without the plating-activation or forming feasibility check
edge_cases.mitigation: confirm an activation-strike plating route and forming feasibility (or wear it bare) before committing 316L

priority_rationale: The substrate-role frame, the EN1811 nickel fact, the 18-25 skin-contact rationale, the corrosion mechanisms and the property-axis schema come first because every substrate judgment depends on knowing what the base metal is responsible for, the real skin-safety standard, and the axes to grade on; the five per-metal profiles then populate those axes; the barrier/plateability, relative-cost, wear-through-safety, appearance/heft, formability and lead/cadmium nodes next, because they are the derived decision axes and vetoes; and the price/quality target matrix, honesty ledger and hand-off come last because they compose the target-dependent substrate choice, its evidence discipline and its conditioned delivery to the finishes and quality-cost KBs.

dominance_rules.rule: Measured nickel release dominates any 'hypoallergenic' or 'surgical steel' label
dominance_rules.rationale: the marketing terms are unregulated and 316L contains nickel; only EN1811 release is a real safety criterion
dominance_rules.trigger: a skin-safety claim rests on a label rather than a test
dominance_rules.action: require an EN1811 (or DMG screen) result, after simulated wear, before the claim

dominance_rules.rule: Skin-safety dominates raw metal cost on skin-contact SKUs
dominance_rules.rationale: a nickel dermatitis reaction durably removes a young buyer and undermines the brand
dominance_rules.trigger: a cheaper substrate/barrier fails the worn EN1811 gate
dominance_rules.action: spend on a nickel-safe substrate or nickel-free barrier rather than ship the cheaper failing piece

dominance_rules.rule: Nickel-safe and nickel-free are distinct and must never be conflated
dominance_rules.rationale: a nickel-free promise made about a nickel-safe (nickel-containing) item misleads a sensitized wearer
dominance_rules.trigger: a nickel-containing item (e.g. 316L, nickel barrier) is described as nickel-free
dominance_rules.action: state nickel-safe with its EN1811 basis, or switch to a genuinely nickel-free stack if the claim requires it

dominance_rules.rule: Lead/cadmium legal limits dominate the cost savings of pot-metal
dominance_rules.rationale: CPSC/state limits are binding US law, unlike nickel which has no US federal limit
dominance_rules.trigger: leaded/cadmium-bearing zinc/pewter is proposed for a skin-contact or children's item
dominance_rules.action: disqualify it; specify and composition-test a low-lead/low-cadmium alloy

dominance_rules.rule: The target-dependent matrix dominates any single 'best base metal' claim
dominance_rules.rationale: each metal wins on different axes, so the best choice depends on the price/quality/skin-safety target
dominance_rules.trigger: a decision asks for one universal best substrate
dominance_rules.action: answer with the target-indexed matrix and its per-cell axis justification

dominance_rules.rule: A barrier under gold on copper/brass is mandatory and dominates a cost-shortcut
dominance_rules.rationale: copper interdiffusion stains and dulls thin gold and the piece fails visually
dominance_rules.trigger: a plan omits the barrier on a copper-bearing substrate to save a step
dominance_rules.action: keep the nickel or nickel-free barrier; it is non-optional on copper/brass

dominance_rules.rule: Method-derived ordinal cost dominates any fabricated per-piece price
dominance_rules.rationale: absolute per-piece cost depends on gauge/weight/plating/MOQ the economics specialist owns
dominance_rules.trigger: an absolute substrate price is asserted as measured
dominance_rules.action: keep cost ordinal and pull live spot by [METHOD]; route absolute COGS to the economics specialist

dominance_rules.rule: Finished (plated, yielded) cost dominates raw commodity cost in tier selection
dominance_rules.rationale: raw-cheap 316L/zinc carry activation-strike and yield penalties that invert the naive ranking
dominance_rules.trigger: substrates are ranked on raw metal price alone
dominance_rules.action: add the plating-difficulty and scrap penalty before comparing tiers

dominance_rules.rule: A category mechanical veto dominates a cost/safety-optimal but unfit substrate
dominance_rules.rationale: a metal that cannot make the part (e.g. pure zinc as a spring post) is disqualified regardless of cost or safety
dominance_rules.trigger: a chosen substrate cannot meet the category's mechanical demand
dominance_rules.action: select a mechanically-fit substrate for the category even at higher cost

anti_rework_rules.rule: Test EN1811 nickel release (after simulated wear) before making any hypoallergenic claim
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a hypoallergenic claim that fails on a worn piece and forces a recall or reputational retraction

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide the nickel-vs-nickel-free barrier at substrate-selection time for copper/brass
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a skin-contact SKU built on a nickel barrier that later fails the worn skin-safety gate and must be re-engineered

anti_rework_rules.rule: Composition-test zinc/pewter against CPSC/state lead-cadmium limits before casting
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a produced lot that breaches lead/cadmium law and cannot be sold for skin-contact/children's use

anti_rework_rules.rule: Rank cost on finished (plated, yielded) cost, not raw commodity price, from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a tier decision built on raw-cheap 316L/zinc that inverts once plating and scrap costs are added

anti_rework_rules.rule: Specify the barrier underplate on any copper-bearing substrate at design time
anti_rework_rules.prevents: gold plated directly on copper/brass interdiffusing and dulling, forcing a re-plate

anti_rework_rules.rule: Match substrate temper/grade to the category's mechanical demand before ordering stock
anti_rework_rules.prevents: ordering a substrate/temper that cannot make the part (soft zinc for a spring post) and re-sourcing

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pick the substrate against the stated price/quality target, not in isolation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: selecting a metal that is wrong for the tier and reworking the whole SKU's material and finish

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every cost/share/prevalence number [FACT]/[ESTIMATE]/[METHOD]/[UNKNOWN] as authored
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a fabricated price or market share propagating into downstream KBs and having to be retracted
